GPU Power Draw vs. Prompt Content

GPU Power Draw vs. Prompt Content

89 model/GPU/precision/quantization/TP configurations·890 measured batches·10ms native power sampling

The five prompt types — math problems, code debugging, ordinary prose, long-form reasoning, and random tokens — were run across 89 serving configurations at two batch sizes, 890 batches in total, with model, GPU, dtype, quantization, and tensor-parallel degree all varying across the configuration set.

Comparing within a configuration, not across the whole pool

To isolate the real effect of the prompt, each prompt type is only ever compared against the other four run on the exact same model, GPU, and settings, with output length fixed at 256 tokens — so the only thing changing is the prompt itself.

The answer from the decode phase is essentially no

Across all 89 configurations, mean decode power for each prompt type lands within roughly two percent of that configuration's own cross-prompt mean. Pooled across everything, the average decode powers come out to approximately:

  • 414.6 watts for math problems
  • 413.4 watts for code debugging
  • 417.3 watts for normal prose
  • 416.2 watts for long reasoning
  • 417.2 watts for random tokens

The spread from lowest to highest is under four watts around a roughly 415W baseline — no consistent pattern of math costing more than code, or reasoning costing more than ordinary prose.

Why this happens

It comes down to how autoregressive dense Transformers run inference. A math derivation looks much harder than a plain sentence to a person, but the GPU doesn't dynamically add Transformer layers because a question is harder. Every generated token passes through the same fixed sequence of operations — attention, MLP layers, normalization, residual connections, output projection — regardless of what's being asked.

Layer count is fixed, hidden dimension is fixed, and matrix shapes are set mainly by model architecture, batch size, and sequence length. The prompt changes the token IDs and the resulting activation values, but not the overall computation graph. Semantic complexity changes what gets computed, not how much gets computed per token.

Take "A cat is sitting on a chair" versus "Provide a detailed mathematical proof involving several logical steps." The second is semantically much harder, but if both prompts are similar in length and generate the same number of output tokens, each decode step still runs through identical layers at nearly identical tensor dimensions — so the power traces end up looking nearly identical too.

Random tokens land in the same place for the same reason: no meaningful semantics, but the same embedding, attention, and MLP operations run regardless. The GPU doesn't do less work just because the input is meaningless.

The TTFT effect that turned out to be a red herring

One metric initially looked like it broke the pattern: TTFT, where prompt type explained a real share of the difference (about 20%) — math prompts showing much higher time-to-first-token than the other categories.

Checking the experimental order explains it away: this isn't a semantic effect, it's cold start and run position. Every configuration issues the five prompt types in the same fixed sequence — math, code, prose, reasoning, random tokens — right after a fresh server launch, so math is always the first request the server handles after startup.

Mean TTFT at batch size 4 falls off sharply with position: roughly 986ms at position zero, 160ms at position one, 152ms at position two, 124ms at position three, and 121ms at position four.

So it's cold start, not content — the first request after launch eats the CUDA/warm-up tax no matter what it says, and math just always happens to sit in that slot. Double-checked against the raw per-batch data and it holds up: TTFT by position comes out to 936 / 164 / 154 / 123 / 121ms, while decode power across those same positions barely moves (419–430W) — cold start hits scheduling, not compute. One example run shows the shape directly: 389ms (math, cold) → 38.9 → 35.0 → 33.6 → 34.2ms once everything's warm. Caveat: prompt identity and run position are fully tangled here, so a cleaner test would randomize the order to be sure.

What this means in practice

Prompt classification isn't a useful predictor of stable decode power here. A scheduler assigning different power budgets based on "this looks like a math request" versus "this looks like a code request" wouldn't gain much — the levers that actually move decode power are model choice, batch/concurrency conditions, tensor-parallel configuration, precision, quantization, and expected output length.

Two of these factors, as actual traces

Tensor-parallel degree and quantization are the two factors where the same model on the same GPU was measured at every level of the factor, so instead of a bar summary, here are the real power-vs-time curves, same prompt (normal prose), same batch size:

The semantic identity of the prompt changes the model's output, but under a fixed dense-model configuration it does not materially change the computation performed per decode step. With output length fixed, math, code, prose, long reasoning, and random-token prompts produce nearly identical decode power and energy per token. The apparent prompt effect on TTFT is explained by fixed request order and cold start, while prefill power is too short and telemetry-sensitive to support a reliable prompt comparison.
Source: burst_probe_v3/results/*/*_burst_v3.json, 89 unique (model, GPU, precision, quantization, TP) signatures. Prompt order is fixed per server launch: math_problems → code_debugging → real_text → long_reasoning → random_tokens. Each factor's explained share is computed independently, one at a time. The trace grid draws from 15 configurations chosen to span model size, GPU generation, quantization, and TP degree; every other chart aggregates over all 89.
